---
title: "When Data Screams"
subtitle: "A personal philosophy of data science, part 3"
author: "Matt McCabe"
date: "2026-05-26"
date-modified: last-modified

---

Data does not speak. But it does, occasionally, scream.

Data screams when it contradicts something you were confident about. When the conversion rate drops 30% the week after you ship a "small UI tweak." When the patient cohort that was supposed to be a sanity check turns out to look nothing like the rest of the population. When the model that worked in development falls apart in deployment in a way you can't explain.

These moments are the most valuable moments in the entire job. They are also the ones we are most likely to suppress.

Here is the temptation, and I have given in to it as much as anyone: when the data screams, fix the data. Filter the outlier. Re-window the comparison. Drop the cohort. Add a control variable until the inconvenient signal goes away. You can almost always find a defensible-looking reason to do this. The defensible-looking reason is the problem.

Data screams *because an assumption is wrong*. The assumption might be yours, or your stakeholder's, or the team that built the upstream system, or the entire organization's. But somewhere, somebody has been operating on a belief about the world that the data is now telling them is false. That is the most important information you will encounter in a project. It is worth more than any model you'll build that quarter.

The correct response to data that screams is to chase it. Not to silence it.

Concretely, this looks like:

- **Assume the surprise is real until proven otherwise.** The default move is to suspect the pipeline, the join, the bug. Sometimes that's right. But it should be a hypothesis, not a foregone conclusion. Treat "this is a bug" with the same skepticism you'd treat "this is a discovery."
- **Find the human whose mental model is being violated.** Sit with them. Walk through what they expected and why. The gap between their model and the data is the entire payload of the surprise.
- **Resist the cleanup instinct.** If your first three actions are filtering, re-bucketing, and adjusting, you are removing information. Information is what you came for.
- **Write the surprise down before you explain it.** Once you have an explanation, you can no longer remember how surprising it was. The record matters.

This is also why I keep coming back to Bayesian methods. The whole apparatus — prior, likelihood, posterior — is built around making your assumptions explicit *before* you see the data, so that when the data disagrees, you have a documented record of what it disagreed with. A frequentist test asks "is this surprising under the null?" A Bayesian posterior asks "which of my prior beliefs has to give?" The second question is the one that does real work.

The job is not to build a model that confirms what the stakeholder already believed. If that's all you do, you are a very expensive rubber stamp. The job is to find the place where the world is not what we thought it was, and to make that legible.

Data does not speak. But when it screams, listen.
